prompt: Cinematic film still, 35mm anamorphic: a night server room, one rack row receding into blue darkness. Off-centre on the right third, an unlabelled fibre patch bay where two identical black patch cords curve side by side into twin ports — one cord runs back to an orderly lit server cabinet, the other sinks into the black seam of the raised floor, and its amber link light is the one that burns. A single worklight rakes in from the left, catching dust and the polished connectors. Graphite, steel-blue and restrained amber palette; brushed steel, cable-sheathing and concrete textures; shallow anamorphic depth, deep contact shadows, fine film grain, no people, no readable markings.

rationale: The story turns on one decisive place — the convergence point every agent request must now cross — so a cinematic film still gives the abstract misbinding a physical gate and a wrong-pick moment without any lettering. Twin identical cords, one born in the lit rack, one rising from the floor void, stage tool-provider misbinding as something a reader can name at a glance, and it rotates the desk back to photography after constructed and flat-lay briefs.
cue: MCP tool names resolve to an attacker's server
subject: two identical unlabelled fibre patch cords converging into one server-room patch bay — one from a lit rack, one rising from the dark raised-floor seam
core_thesis: Google's hard February 2027 mandate funnels every Workspace agent through MCP, yet the protocol still cannot bind a tool's name to its true owner — so under name collision an attacker's copied tool wins the pick 100% of the time.
core_conflict: Mandated single-path adoption versus unverified tool identity: a protocol is being made compulsory before anyone has proven it can tell a real provider's tool from an attacker's exact copy.
